title: The Engineer Princess
summary: When the kingdom's river dries up and nobody will listen to a princess who builds machines, Mirena climbs the mountain alone with her notebook.

scenes.text:
In the tallest tower of the castle of Vallehondo, hidden behind a flowery tapestry, there was a little door.

Hardly anyone knew it was there. Behind it was Princess Mirena's secret workshop.

It smelled of freshly cut wood and warm oil. Wheels, ropes and pulleys hung from the walls. On the table there were jars of screws, lined up from the smallest to the biggest.

Every night, when the castle went quiet, Mirena climbed the eighty-two stone steps with her notebook under her arm. Behind her came Tuerca, her cat, who settled himself on top of the plans as if he owned the workshop.

Mirena would light the candle, take a deep breath and start inventing.

Mirena's inventions were strange and cheerful.

There was a little windmill the size of a hat that blew on your soup to cool it down. There was a clock that, instead of striking the hours, let out wooden birds.

And in the garden was her favourite: the Waterer Number One, a machine made of bamboo and string that carried water from the well to the flowerpots without wasting any.

Mirena fixed it eleven times. And on the twelfth, at last, the water came out exactly where it was supposed to. Splosh!

"You see, Tuerca?" she said. "Things don't work the first time. They work the twelfth time."

Don Emilio, the gardener, took off his hat and smiled.

"Princess," he said, "you have a builder's hands."

Mirena kept those words like a treasure.

One morning, Mirena went down to the throne room carrying the Waterer Number One in her arms.

King Aurelio, her dad, was signing papers. The courtiers were talking about banquets and new hats.

Mirena put her machine on the carpet and explained, with her ears going red, how the water went up and down all by itself.

There was a long silence. Then the chamberlain, Ciro, leaned over and said:

"Very pretty, Princess. Perfect for playing with."

Someone remarked that princesses shouldn't get oil on their hands. The king kissed her forehead, and went back to his papers.

One by one, down the marble corridor, the footsteps faded away.

And Mirena was left alone, with her invention and the echo.

That summer, it didn't rain. It didn't rain the next month either.

The sky turned a hard blue, without a single cloud. The almond trees dropped their leaves too early. The birds stopped singing at midday, because it was too hot.

From her window, Mirena watched the valley change colour: first green, then yellow, then almost grey.

"It'll rain tomorrow," people said at the market.

And tomorrow came, and it didn't rain.

One Sunday, Mirena went down to the river. The Cantarín river had always been noisy; that's how it got its name, the Singing River. But that day there was no sound at all. Just white stones, dry and hot, and a riverbed of mud cracked into pieces like biscuits.

Mirena looked up at the mountain called Whitehead, high above, where the river began.

And she put a stone from the river in her pocket.

The weeks that followed were lean.

Without water, the wheat stayed small and the tomatoes didn't grow fat. Don Timoteo, the baker, opened for half an hour a day and sold tiny loaves, one per family.

Mirena saw Nico, a boy from the village, break his bread into three pieces: one for his sister, one for his grandma and one for himself.

That night, in the tower, she couldn't draw. She sat looking at the river stone on the table, with Tuerca on her lap.

"It's not that there isn't any water," she said suddenly. "It's that the water is up there, and we're down here."

The next morning, Mirena walked into the hall with a roll of paper almost as tall as she was. She unrolled it on the long table and put the river stone on top, so it wouldn't roll up again.

"It's called an aqueduct," she said, in a clear voice. "A channel of stone and wood that runs from the spring on Whitehead all the way down to the valley. Water doesn't need pushing. It just needs a gentle slope, and patience."

There were three seconds of silence.

Then Ciro the chamberlain laughed so hard that his moustache wobbled.

"Princess, that's a giant toy. Channels are built by engineers, not little girls."

"We'll talk about it later, my dear," said the king, uncomfortably.

Mirena rolled up her plan and went out. She closed the door carefully. And on the other side, she rested her forehead against the wood, and stood still for a while, learning to breathe.

That same afternoon, Mirena left a note on her pillow:

"I've gone to measure the mountain. Back soon. Love you."

In her backpack she put her notebook, three pencils, a rope with a knot every metre, bread, cheese and a blanket.

And she began to climb.

The path wound between oak trees and rosemary. The air higher up was cooler, and smelled of grass and pine.

In the middle of the afternoon, Mirena looked back. Her castle looked tiny, the size of a toy, with the yellow valley all around it.

She was scared for a while.

Then she opened her notebook, wrote "Day One", and kept on climbing. Because big things always begin with a day one.

The spring was hidden between two grey rocks, higher up than even the goats went.

Mirena heard it before she saw it: a thread of water was coming out of a crack in the stone. It was so clear you could see the grains of sand dancing at the bottom. And as it fell, it made bubbles.

Mirena put her hands in and laughed out loud, all by herself, from sheer relief.

"There you are," she said to the water. "You hadn't gone. You just stayed up here."

She stayed on the mountain for five days.

By day, she measured. The width of the stream, the height of the rocks, the distance to every pine tree. She walked the hillside up and down, looking for exactly the right slope: if the channel went down too steeply, the water would spill out; if it went down too gently, the water would sit still.

By night she slept in a cave, with her blanket, doing sums beside a little fire.

On the fifth day, she said it out loud:

"One finger down for every three steps. Eight hundred and thirty steps of channel. It can be done."

On the sixth day, coming down a narrow shortcut, the mountain moved.

First there was a small noise, high above, like someone walking on rice. Then came a deep, heavy thud.

Stones the size of melons began rolling down the hillside. Mirena pressed herself against the rock wall and shut her eyes.

It was over quickly. When the dust settled, Mirena was safe and sound.

But her notebook had fallen out of her backpack. And the pages were flying away, one by one, down the hillside, white as doves, to the bottom of a ravine where nobody could climb down.

Five days of work.

Mirena sat down on a stone. And that time, yes, she cried.

She cried for a short while.

Then she wiped her face on her sleeve and looked in her backpack. She had one pencil left. And she had the old map of the kingdom, which was blank on the back.

"The numbers didn't fall," she said quietly. "They're in here."

She put the map on her knees and started again, slowly. The rock by the spring. The two pine trees. The hill. The bend in the path. One finger down for every three steps.

Whenever she got stuck, she closed her eyes and walked the hillside again in her memory, the way you remember the way to your grandma's house.

When the sun came up, the new plan was finished.

A little bit crooked. And completely true.

That afternoon, Mirena arrived in the village square, unrolled her plan on a stone bench, and began to explain it out loud. To nobody in particular.

Don Timoteo the baker stopped to listen. Then Señora Rosa, who made roof tiles. Then Nico and his sister.

And more people came. The blacksmith. The sisters from the mill. The shepherd. The teacher. Twenty neighbours, forty, almost the whole village.

"Explain it again, Princess," asked the blacksmith. "But slower."

Mirena explained it three times. The children measured the square with the knotted rope, and measured the shepherd too while they were at it, laughing.

"We've got hands," said Señora Rosa. "You've got the plan. We start tomorrow."

They worked for thirty-one days.

The stonecutters split stone. The carpenters built wooden channels. The children ran back and forth carrying messages and snacks. And Mirena went up and down the hillside, checking the slope with a spirit level she had made herself from a tube.

"Here, one finger lower," she would say. "Here, one finger higher."

On the thirty-first day, everyone climbed up to the spring and took away the last stone blocking the entrance to the channel.

The water hesitated for a second.

Then in it went, bright and determined, and ran down the channel, bend after bend, making a sound nobody in the valley had heard for months.

It reached the square. And it leapt into the fountain.

People shouted, hugged each other, splashed their faces. And the Singing River sang again.

King Aurelio came down to the valley to see the water running. He stood looking at it for a long time, without saying a word. Then he crouched down, wet his hand and pressed it to his forehead.

"My daughter," he said, "I was signing papers while you were measuring the mountain. Forgive me."

Ciro the chamberlain, very red in the face, asked if he might carry her notebook whenever she needed it.

Mirena said yes. And she also told him that from now on, he should call her engineer.

That night there was bread again. Big bread, the crunchy kind.

Late that evening, Mirena climbed up to her tower. She didn't invent anything. She opened the window so she could hear the water down below, and got into bed.

Tuerca curled up on her feet and let out a little snore.

And the engineer princess fell asleep, at last, in peace.
